title: One pawn move and the bishop: which rule holds
outcomes: Predicts whether a given pawn move costs a bishop moves, by checking its colour and its diagonals
Tells the count rule (pawns on the bishop's colour) from the bishop's actual moves
Says which of the two bishop-and-pawn colour rules has support here, and at what evidence grade

steps.text: In *Good and bad pieces: now, and later* you counted a bishop's squares. A count rule says: a bishop is **bad** when more than half its side's pawns stand on its colour, so a pawn move can change the verdict, and sometimes the verdict and the real moves disagree. Two rules compete: keep pawns off your own bishop's colour, or put pawns on the colour of the enemy bishop. Test the first on a board.

steps.caption: White to move. The bishop on d3 moves on light squares.

line.say: e4 stands on the bishop's diagonal: 10 legal moves become 6, yet the count rule still calls it good (3 of 8 pawns).

claims.statement: The White bishop stands on d3.
White has 2 pawns on light squares and 6 on dark squares.
After e4: 3 on light squares and 5 on dark squares.

steps.text: **What the checks show.** Rule one (keep your pawns off your own bishop's colour) comes from Capablanca's book [S], one source, and a pawn on the bishop's diagonal cost it moves here [V]; whether it wins games is untested [H]. Rule two (pawns on the enemy bishop's colour) is a hypothesis [H]. The count is a **rule of thumb**: a pawn on the bishop's colour off its diagonals may cost nothing.
